Okay, put simply, can one bleed across the table using Computer
Hacking (and other (D) bleed cards)?

My thinking is "no" since I think the (D) is there as a reminder that
bleeds are a directed action and not as a method to change the valid
target of the action (which, by default, is your prey ). Thus, unless
the card specifies that a bleed can be directed at anyone, bleeds can
only be targeted at your prey.

However, others have tried to convince me otherwise and I almost
believe them.

Thanks,

Also, the original rule AND the original intent was for bleeds to always
be directed at your prey unless explicitly said otherwise (like, superior
Cat Burglary).
Changing it to be allowing bleeds to everyone was found my experience to
detract from the game.
It's a mistake that has been rectified. We'd all be better off,
certainly, if the RT had never made the change in the first place, since
then this wouldn't be an issue. (Not really, I know, since groups made that
ruling for themselves in a RT vacuum and failing to read the rulebook
carefully.)

so you seem to think that bleeding anyone on the table is just okay.
I maintain that keeping a strong Prey/predator relationship between player
makes this game interesting and fun to play. "Everyone Beat the weaker to a
pulp" has nothing to do there, because you have (most of the time) no
interest in killing a guy crosstable. You even might want to help him with
powerbase access or replenishing vote. without the prey/predator style of
play, there's no almost no place for politics or alliance.
the first change of the rule (bleed directed wherever you want) was a
mistake.
the return to original rule is a good thing, because it reflects the true
spirit of the jyhad : you have a grief on a particular methuselah, and you
are the target of another one. It's the main theme of the game.

so it has to do with the discussion. I still can read plain english.

Messages.Author: LSJ

Talo...@hotmail.com wrote:
> Yes, but if you'll recall, that was in reference to D bleed action
> cards like computer hacking. Most 'bleed at' include 'bleed your prey
> at' text these days.
>
> Only a few open ended D bleed cards remain. Those made the game
> interesting when you could bleed across the table.

You can still use the open-ended bleed actions (superior Cat
Burglary and Kindred Spirits) to bleed across table.

The only thing that has changed is that the errata that gave
a subset of the (D) symbols printed on action cards the ability to
grant omnidirectability (in opposition to the printed rulebooks and
the stated intention of the game designer) has been reversed. Now
the (D) symbol represents a reminder, just like the rulebooks have
said.

> [snip]

> Allowing a few cards to cross table bleed shouldnt prevent this.

A few are allowed. See superior Cat Burglary and Kindred Spirits.

Ah, I'm not sure I agree with James in how he defended the rule. You're
right - that is pretty fuzzy stuff.

Personally, I like the rule simply because there's enough politics
and ganging up against the lead player as it is without allowing lots
of extra cross-table bleed cards. (Which may have been approximately
what James was trying to say.) Rush combat decks can do a lot of cross-
table stuff which is probably a good thing, since they don't do well in
so many other ways. Handing bleed decks another tool for winning the
game is simply not necessary - they're strong enough as it is!

> Frankly, it makes sense from both a 'realism' perspective and even to
> further 'collusion' amongst the players to allow D bleeds across the
> table.

Well, that's the thing. It's a matter of taste, of course. But I
don't see why 'collusion' amongst players needs furthering.

Fred

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
Talo...@hotmail.com writes:

> I just remember being able to use computer hacking for the occasional
> 'backbiter' bleed, and it was fun. At the time that was one of the
> few cards you could do that with.

Indeed, a few backbiter bleeds used sensibly by a player were often
quite useful. Howevre, the use of random "I'm annoyed" type bleeds or
"I'm gonna bleed you cos I don't like you" type bleeds are a major
problem - especially considering that bleeds are, of the three major
archetypes (bleed, combat, vote) the most directly powerful.

Richard Garfield, in his introduction to the White Wolf strategy
guide, noted the use of the predator prey dynamic to focus the game.
IT stops the game becoming purely diplomacy, since people really need
the right cards to step outside the dynamic, whicmeans that skill in
the game becomes an imoprtant asset.
